title: Creation begins
hook: by His will the play begins (Sukhmani 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, before creation, and your line: he alone was. When a worry came, did you ask what was there before it? The stillness has lasted two days. Today, something moves. Day five hundred twenty.

A blank document, and a cursor blinking. Blink. Blink. Anyone who has ever had to write something knows that cursor. Everything you could say is still possible, and nothing has been said. Then you type the first word, and suddenly there's a direction, a voice, a shape. The page will never be blank in quite the same way again. After two days of stillness, the twenty-first ashtpadi reaches its first word. Creation begins.
screen: `THE CURSOR BLINKING.` → `THE FIRST WORD TYPED.` → `CREATION BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The stanzas of the twenty-first ashtpadi keep asking what was there before, and then, near the end, the scene changes. In paraphrase: when He Himself fashioned the world of forms, He spread it out through the three qualities; then sin and virtue came to be spoken of, some went to hell and some longed for heaven. Here's the shape of it. First the stillness, sunn. Then, by God's own choice, forms. And only then all the things that fill our lives: right and wrong, reward and loss, hope and fear. They arrive with the world, not before it. The three qualities, the trigun, are an old Indian idea that Gurbani uses often: everything made is woven from three strands, roughly calm, restless and heavy. Gurbani treats them as part of the made world, which God stands beyond. What sets it all going? Sikh teaching answers with one word: hukam, God's will or order. Guru Nanak says in Japji, in paraphrase: by His hukam forms are created; the hukam can't be described. And the picture Sukhmani keeps returning to is a play, khel. God sets His own khel in motion, and is in it. That word matters. A play isn't a machine, ground out because it must be. It's something made freely, with delight. Sikh teaching doesn't say why God began the play, beyond that it was God's will. It leaves the why with the One who began it.
screen: `FIRST THE STILLNESS, THEN FORMS.` · `RIGHT AND WRONG ARRIVE WITH THE WORLD.` · `HUKAM: BY HIS WILL.` · `KHEL: MADE FREELY, LIKE A PLAY.` · then, large: `THE PLAY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin something small. Sit for a moment in stillness first, the way the ashtpadi did. Then choose one tiny beginning you can make right now: the first sentence of a letter, the first stretch of a walk, the first step of a recipe, one line in a notebook. Make it. Notice the shift from nothing to something, and that you didn't need to know the ending to start. If you pray, you can begin with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Khel, play or game: by God's hukam the stillness gives way to forms, and the world, with all its right and wrong, starts as God's own khel.
Your line: the play begins. Today, start the thing you've been putting off with just its first small step, and let it be a beginning. Day five hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear creation begin by God's hukam, as God's own play, after the stillness of sunn.

pairs: the three qualities of the made world

myth: in Sukhmani, right and wrong existed before the world
they come to be spoken of only once forms are made.
Sukhmani pictures creation as God's own play
khel: something made freely, which God is in.
Gurbani explains exactly why God began creating
it says it was God's will, hukam, and leaves the why with God.

fork.setup: the stillness of sunn gives way to a world. by Sukhmani and Japji, what sets it going?
fork.reveal: hukam. Japji says forms are made by His hukam, and the hukam can't be described. Sukhmani calls the result God's own khel, play.

original.note: Gurmukhi: khel, play or game; Gurbani calls creation God's own khel.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation begins is a story about the first day.
what it means: by God's hukam the stillness gives way to forms, and with them right, wrong, joy and sorrow, as God's play.
what a scholar hears: Sukhmani places sin, virtue, heaven and hell inside the three-stranded made world, the trigun, which God stands beyond.
